findings.claim: 'By 1954 it had around 400,000 members' (the NAACP).
findings.truth: NAACP membership was 351,000 in 1945 and 302,000 in 1958; it fell through the early 1950s. Around 300,000 in the mid-1950s is the supportable figure.

findings.claim: 'Examiners reward inference plus a quoted detail; paragraphs of paraphrase cap at the lower band.'
findings.truth: The 4-mark inference question is point-marked - one mark for each inference and one for the detail that supports it. It has no bands, as the lesson's own mark scheme says.
findings.evidence: spec, Paper 3 assessment information (Section A, Question 1, AO3)

findings.claim: Source A: 'From a 1953 NAACP report to its annual conference describing voter registration in Mississippi', with the figure '121 of 12,000'.
findings.truth: No such report exists; the text and the figures are composed. The invented archive provenance is stripped and the source is labelled as written for the exercise.

findings.claim: Source B: 'From a 1952 letter by Thurgood Marshall ... to a colleague preparing the school cases'.
findings.truth: Composed words put into a real person's mouth and cited as a real letter. Provenance stripped; the attribution to Marshall's position is kept.

findings.claim: 'his eight-year-old daughter Linda at the all-white Sumner Elementary School, four blocks from the family home'.
findings.truth: Sumner was seven blocks from the Brown home. Linda's age at the attempt is disputed (7 in 1950, 8 in 1951), so the age is dropped.

findings.claim: Period vocabulary 'is rewarded under SPaG-adjacent marking on the longer questions'.
findings.truth: On this paper the 4 SPaG marks are attached to one question only - the final evaluate-an-interpretation question. The 12-mark causation question carries none.
findings.evidence: spec, Paper 3 assessment information (Section B, up to 4 SPaG marks in Question 3(d))

findings.claim: 'Rosa Parks's planned arrest'.
findings.truth: Her arrest was not planned. What was planned was the Women's Political Council's readiness to use the right test case, as the lesson body itself explains.

findings.claim: Parks 'had spent much of 1955 at the Highlander Folk School in Tennessee studying nonviolent direct action'.
findings.truth: She attended a short workshop at Highlander in the summer of 1955.

findings.claim: 'Jo Ann Robinson and three of her students mimeographed 35,000 leaflets'.
findings.truth: Robinson worked with two Alabama State College students, using a mimeograph provided by the business department chair.

findings.claim: 'On the evening of 5 December ... leaders met at Holt Street Baptist Church ... They formed the MIA and elected as its president' King. Repeated as the premise of knowledge check 1.
findings.truth: The MIA was formed and King elected at the afternoon meeting at Mount Zion AME Zion Church. Holt Street Baptist Church was the evening mass meeting where King spoke.

findings.claim: Source B: 'From the autobiography of E. D. Nixon'.
findings.truth: Nixon published no autobiography; the passage is composed. Provenance stripped.

findings.claim: Source A: 'From Jet magazine, 15 September 1955', with composed reportage and an invented list of mourners' home towns.
findings.truth: Jet did publish the funeral photographs in its 15 September 1955 issue, but this text is not from it. Provenance stripped.

findings.claim: Source B: 'From the diary of Melba Pattillo Beals ... written during her first weeks at Central High School in September 1957'.
findings.truth: Beals published a memoir, Warriors Don't Cry (1994); no contemporaneous diary is in print, and the wording is composed. Provenance stripped, attribution kept.

findings.claim: Inside Source B and quoted again in its mark scheme: 'The eight of us decided that if we cried, the year was lost.'
findings.truth: There were nine students and all nine were still at the school in September 1957; Minnijean Brown was not expelled until February 1958.

findings.claim: 'Over the summer of 1961 more than 400 Freedom Riders were arrested.'
findings.truth: About 436 people took part in the rides; more than 300 were arrested in Jackson. The 400-plus figure is the participation total, not the arrest total.

findings.claim: Source A: 'From a leaflet distributed by SNCC organisers to potential Freedom Riders in spring 1961'.
findings.truth: CORE organised and launched the 1961 rides, as the lesson body states; SNCC supplied the second wave after Anniston. Organisation corrected and provenance stripped.
findings.evidence: spec Key topic 2.1 (Freedom Riders); lesson body

findings.claim: Source B: 'From a 1962 letter by James Meredith to the US Department of Justice'.
findings.truth: Composed words cited as a real letter from a named living plaintiff to a named federal department. Provenance stripped.

findings.claim: At the March on Washington, 'around 250,000 people, roughly 60 per cent of them Black'.
findings.truth: Observers estimated 75-80 per cent of the marchers were Black.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom'

findings.claim: 'never judge usefulness on bias alone, which caps at the threshold band'.
findings.truth: An invented banding consequence. The real point is that one-sidedness can itself make a source useful, judged against content, provenance and context.
findings.evidence: spec, Paper 3 Question 3(a) (usefulness of two contemporary sources, AO3)

findings.claim: Source A: 'From a 7 May 1963 internal White House memorandum to President Kennedy', including 'Calls and telegrams ... running ten to one'.
findings.truth: A fabricated official document with fabricated statistics. Provenance stripped.

findings.claim: Source B: 'From a press release issued by SNCC on 22 June 1964'.
findings.truth: A fabricated dated organisational document. Provenance stripped.

findings.claim: 'By the end of January 1965, 2,000 Black activists had been arrested, including King himself.'
findings.truth: King was arrested in Selma on 1 February 1965. About 3,000 had been arrested by the end of February.

findings.claim: On Bloody Sunday, 'Around 60 marchers were hospitalised.'
findings.truth: Seventeen marchers were hospitalised and about fifty more were treated for lesser injuries.

findings.claim: Of the quarter of a million voters added to the rolls after the Voting Rights Act, 'Federal registrars enrolled half of them.'
findings.truth: About a third. The lesson's own Source B gives 80,000 enrolled by federal examiners against 170,000 by local boards.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with the lesson's Source B

findings.claim: 'An ‘explain the importance’ question rewards a clear judgement ...'
findings.truth: There is no 'explain the importance' question on this paper. The causation question is the 12-mark 'Explain why'. The rest of the tip already describes that question.
findings.evidence: spec, Paper 3 assessment information (Question 2, AO1/AO2 causation)

findings.claim: Source A: 'From the testimony of John Lewis ... to a US Senate subcommittee in 1965'.
findings.truth: No such testimony; the passage is composed. Provenance stripped, attribution to Lewis kept because the body of the source identifies him.

findings.claim: Source B: 'From a US Civil Rights Commission report published in late 1965', with '26 of the 27 counties'.
findings.truth: A fabricated federal report with invented county figures. Provenance stripped.

findings.claim: Malcolm Little 'was sentenced to ten years in prison for burglary'.
findings.truth: He was sentenced to eight to ten years for larceny and breaking and entering.

findings.claim: 'three Nation of Islam members were eventually convicted of the killing' (of Malcolm X).
findings.truth: Three men were convicted, but Muhammad Aziz and Khalil Islam were exonerated in November 2021 after evidence withheld by the FBI and NYPD came to light.

findings.claim: Source A: 'From a Malcolm X speech delivered at the Audubon Ballroom in Harlem on 14 February 1965, the day his home was firebombed'.
findings.truth: The speech is composed, and on the evening of 14 February 1965 Malcolm spoke in Detroit, not at the Audubon Ballroom. Provenance stripped.
findings.evidence: brief: strip invented archive provenances; Wikipedia 'Malcolm X'

findings.claim: Source B: 'From a 1965 letter Malcolm X wrote home from Mecca during his Hajj'.
findings.truth: The quoted letter is genuine but was written during the Hajj in April 1964. Only the Autobiography is 1965.

findings.claim: 'Twelve days after ... the Tlatelolco massacre, two Black American sprinters stood on the medal rostrum'.
findings.truth: Tlatelolco was 2 October 1968 and the 200m medal ceremony 16 October 1968 - fourteen days.

findings.claim: 'Smith's scarf and Carlos's beads remembered Black Americans who had been lynched' (repeated in the key fact).
findings.truth: Carlos's beads were for lynching victims; Smith's black scarf stood for Black pride.

findings.claim: 'the International Olympic Committee, under pressure from its president Avery Brundage, expelled Smith and Carlos' (repeated in a flashcard).
findings.truth: The US Olympic Committee expelled them, after first refusing and after IOC president Brundage threatened to ban the whole US track team.

findings.claim: Source A: 'From a New York Times news report by William Borders ... published 17 October 1968'.
findings.truth: A composed report given a real newspaper and a real journalist's byline. Provenance stripped.

findings.claim: Mark scheme: 'J. Edgar Hoover's 1968 description of the Panthers as the greatest threat to the internal security of the country'.
findings.truth: Hoover said it in 1969. The lesson body already dates it 'by 1970'.

findings.claim: 'In July 1967 alone there were over 150 incidents'.
findings.truth: The 150-plus figure covers 1967 as a whole (the Kerner Commission counted 164 disorders in the first nine months). July alone saw far fewer.
findings.evidence: Kerner Report count as reported in Wikipedia 'Long, hot summer of 1967'

findings.claim: 'within four months a presidential campaign ... had elected Richard Nixon'.
findings.truth: The Kerner Report appeared on 29 February 1968; Nixon was elected on 5 November 1968, eight months later.

findings.claim: Source B: 'From a Memphis Commercial Appeal news report ... published 5 April 1968'.
findings.truth: A composed report attributed to a real newspaper on a real date. Provenance stripped.

findings.claim: Dien Bien Phu 'ended sixty-four years of French colonial rule in Indochina'.
findings.truth: No start date gives 64 years: French rule dates from the 1880s conquest and the 1887 Indochinese Union, so about 67-70 years.

findings.claim: 'the Republic of Vietnam under Bao Dai in Saigon, and from 1955 under Ngo Dinh Diem'.
findings.truth: The southern state in 1954 was the State of Vietnam under Bao Dai. The Republic of Vietnam was proclaimed in October 1955 under Diem.

findings.claim: 'the live televised self-immolation of the monk Thich Quang Duc'.
findings.truth: It was not broadcast live. Malcolm Browne's photographs carried it to front pages worldwide.

findings.claim: 'by August 1964 South Vietnam's government had collapsed nine times in nine months'.
findings.truth: Contradicts the lesson's own claim of nine successive juntas in the first eighteen months after the November 1963 coup.

findings.claim: Source A adds to Eisenhower's genuine 7 April 1954 press conference: 'The loss of Indochina will cause the fall of Southeast Asia like a set of dominoes.'
findings.truth: That sentence is not in the transcript. The rest of the quotation is genuine, so only the interpolation is removed.

findings.claim: Source B: 'From a memorandum of conversation between US ambassador Henry Cabot Lodge and Vice President Lyndon B. Johnson, 25 October 1963'.
findings.truth: A fabricated dated official record naming two real officials. Provenance stripped.

findings.claim: Source A: 'From a US Army training pamphlet for soldiers arriving in South Vietnam, 1967', containing 'The body count is your scorecard.'
findings.truth: No such pamphlet; the passage puts composed instructions into an official military document. Provenance stripped.

findings.claim: 'There was, he said in a White House press conference in November, ‘light at the end of the tunnel’.'
findings.truth: Westmoreland spoke at the National Press Club on 21 November 1967 and said 'We have reached an important point when the end begins to come into view'. 'Light at the end of the tunnel' is the press shorthand, not his words.

findings.claim: Cronkite 'closed his programme by telling viewers that the war would ‘end in stalemate’'; the glossary adds 'broadcast from Saigon'.
findings.truth: His words were 'To say that we are mired in stalemate seems the only realistic, yet unsatisfactory, conclusion', delivered after he returned from Vietnam.

findings.claim: 'a contingent of around seventy-seven guardsmen ... opened fire ... They fired sixty-seven rounds'.
findings.truth: Seventy-seven guardsmen advanced; twenty-eight of them fired the 67 rounds.

findings.claim: Source A: 'From a private memorandum from Defense Secretary Clark Clifford to President Lyndon B. Johnson, 4 March 1968'.
findings.truth: A fabricated dated memorandum naming a real official. Provenance stripped.

findings.claim: Source B: 'From a 1971 letter from a Kent State University professor ... written shortly after the 4 May 1970 shootings'.
findings.truth: Invented provenance, and internally contradictory: a 1971 letter cannot have been written shortly after May 1970. Provenance stripped and the date fixed.

findings.claim: Source A: 'From an internal memorandum from Henry Kissinger to President Nixon, 10 September 1971'.
findings.truth: A fabricated dated memorandum naming a real official. Provenance stripped.

findings.claim: 'the Pittsburgh Courier called it ‘the second emancipation’'.
findings.truth: Not found in the reachable sources on either the Pittsburgh Courier or the Chicago Defender. Left alone under the rule that an unverified quotation is never a FIX, but it should be checked against a print source before the next narration.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Pittsburgh Courier', Wikipedia 'The Chicago Defender' (neither records it)

findings.claim: bombings 'became known as ‘the Mississippi state flower’ in some Black communities'.
findings.truth: No source found for this nickname. Colourful and unverifiable; worth cutting if it cannot be sourced.

findings.claim: Medgar Evers 'would himself be assassinated by a Klan-aligned killer in 1963'.
findings.truth: Byron De La Beckwith joined his local White Citizens' Council in 1954; the date he joined the Klan is not established, so 'Klan-aligned' in 1963 is unsupported. The lesson's own three-layer framework makes the distinction matter.

findings.claim: 'By 1959 the Nation had grown from around 400 members in 1952 to perhaps 50,000.'
findings.truth: Estimates vary widely: about 1,200 in the early 1950s rising to between 50,000 and 100,000 nominal members by the early 1960s, with about 25,000 attending. The lesson's figures sit at the low end and are dated early.

findings.claim: 'Westmoreland told a press conference in early February that he had ‘defeated the enemy's will to win’.'
findings.truth: Not found in the reachable sources; his documented early-February line was that Tet was a diversion ahead of Khe Sanh. Left as a NOTE because the quotation could not be disproved.

findings.claim: 'Johnson reportedly told an aide that if he had lost Cronkite, he had lost ‘Mr Average Citizen’.'
findings.truth: The usual reported wording is 'Middle America', and the whole story is disputed - Johnson was in Austin when the editorial aired. The lesson already hedges with 'reportedly'.

findings.claim: The final evaluate-an-interpretation question is labelled '16 marks' in nine lessons and '20 marks ... (with SPaG)' in five (lessons 2, 4, 8, 9, 14).
findings.truth: Both labels are accurate - 16 for the argument plus up to 4 for SPaG - but a student meets the same question at two different tariffs. Recommend normalising on '16 marks' with the SPaG allowance named in the mark scheme. Lessons 2 and 4 also carry the meaningless student instruction '(You may include any SPaG mark separately.)'.
findings.evidence: spec, Paper 3 Section B (36 marks: 8 + 4 + 4 + 16, plus up to 4 SPaG in the last part)
findings.ruling: Leave (both readings true / ripple not worth it).

findings.claim: Every interpretation pair is composed and attributed generically ('from a 2010 study of ...').
findings.truth: This is the normal exam-practice convention and names no real historian or work, so it is left alone. Only sources with invented specific provenance were changed.
findings.evidence: brief: label composed sources or interpretations only as a NOTE

findings.claim: Operation Rolling Thunder given as ending '31 October 1968' in the content, key fact, glossary and a flashcard.
findings.truth: 31 October 1968 is the date Johnson announced the halt; the campaign is usually dated to 2 November 1968. Either is defensible and correcting it would ripple through four fields, so it is left for a decision.
findings.ruling: Leave (both readings true / ripple not worth it).

findings.claim: Kissinger described as 'Architect of Vietnamisation'.
findings.truth: Vietnamisation was named and driven by Defense Secretary Melvin Laird. GCSE textbooks routinely credit Nixon and Kissinger, so this is recorded rather than changed.
findings.evidence: standard accounts of the Nixon administration

findings.claim: The composed Source A glosses the bowed heads as being 'for the lynched'.
findings.truth: Smith's own account attaches the lynching reference to Carlos's beads. The lesson narrative is corrected by F33; the source is left because its mark scheme quotes the phrase.

findings.claim: 'end in stalemate' survives as Cronkite's words in the credibility-gap glossary entry, a knowledge check option, a flashcard, the exam tip and Interpretation 1.
findings.truth: F48 corrects the narrative and the Cronkite glossary entry so a student meets the real wording once. Replacing the shorthand everywhere would rewrite a knowledge check, a flashcard and an interpretation extract - worth doing only if the whole shorthand is to be retired.
findings.ruling: Leave (both readings true / ripple not worth it).

findings.claim: 'James Meredith, a 29-year-old Air Force veteran, applied to the University of Mississippi ... in 1961.'
findings.truth: Meredith applied in January 1961 aged 27; he was 29 during the September-October 1962 crisis.

summary: Fourteen lessons checked. Unlike the sibling Weimar unit the exam furniture is broadly right - the Paper 3 forms and the 4/12/8/4/4/16 tariffs are correct throughout - so the damage sits elsewhere. Thirteen of the fourteen lessons carry composed sources dressed in invented archive provenance (a Jet article, a New York Times byline, a White House memorandum, a Kissinger memo, a Melba Pattillo Beals diary, an E. D. Nixon autobiography, testimony by John Lewis), all now stripped and labelled. Sixteen dates and figures are wrong and mark-affecting: NAACP membership, Sumner's distance, the Montgomery Improvement Association's founding venue, Freedom Rider arrests, the March on Washington's racial composition, Bloody Sunday hospitalisations, King's Selma arrest, the federal-registrar share, the Tlatelolco interval, the Olympic salute's symbolism and who expelled Smith and Carlos, the 1967 riot count, the Nixon election interval, French rule in Indochina, the State of Vietnam, Thich Quang Duc's photograph and the Kent State firing party. Four exam claims were invented banding or the wrong question type - one lesson taught the 12-mark 'Explain why' as an 'explain the importance' question from another paper. Two direct quotations were wrong: Westmoreland's National Press Club line and Cronkite's stalemate conclusion.
